analysis.investment_thesis: KPI Green Energy is a high-growth renewable energy IPP with strong revenue momentum, but its debt/equity of 0.88 — nearly 3x my maximum threshold — and persistently negative free cash flow every single year make this a business I cannot own. Explosive 92% revenue CAGR funded entirely by borrowings and equity dilution is not compounding; it is leveraged construction.
key_strengths: Robust operating margins of 30.6% with consistent EBITDA expansion from ₹19 Cr to ₹575 Cr in 6 years
ROE of 19.7% and ROCE of 17.5% are above my 15% threshold, reflecting decent capital utilisation
India's renewable energy tailwind provides long-duration demand visibility for IPPs with PPAs
key_risks: Debt/Equity of 0.88 with borrowings exploding from ₹139 Cr to ₹2,533 Cr — completely outside my 0.3 limit
Free cash flow negative every year (-₹1,297 Cr in FY25) — the business consumes cash, not generates it
Promoter holding at 49.49% is below my 55% floor, and the massive equity dilution (reserves from ₹80 Cr to ₹2,551 Cr) signals dependence on capital markets
red_flags: Debt/Equity 0.88 — unacceptable, exceeds my hard limit of 0.3 by nearly 3x
FCF negative all 5 years (cumulative -₹1,870 Cr) — the business is a cash incinerator funded by lenders and equity markets
Capex of ₹1,505 Cr in FY25 alone against OCF of ₹208 Cr — structurally dependent on external capital
Aggressive expansion funded by debt — a pattern I have seen destroy wealth in infrastructure cycles
analysis.detailed_analysis:
KPI Green Energy fails my most fundamental test before I even look at the income statement: the balance sheet is leveraged beyond recognition for my comfort. Borrowings have grown 18x in five years to ₹2,533 Cr, and at D/E of 0.88 this company is running close to 1:1 debt-to-equity. I built DMart by refusing to take on debt — I have seen what happens to capital-heavy businesses when interest rates rise, power purchase agreements are renegotiated, or capacity additions slow down. Finance costs of ₹79 Cr (FY25) are still substantial, and CWIP has ballooned to ₹709 Cr, signalling even more capital commitment ahead.

Beyond the balance sheet, this is simply not a business I understand or prefer. I like consumer-facing businesses with predictable, recurring, low-capital demand — retail, FMCG, private banking. An independent power producer with lumpy capex, regulatory tariff risk, land acquisition complexity, and no dividend (because FCF is negative) is the opposite of what I look for. The 92.6% revenue CAGR is impressive but it is build-and-leverage growth, not organic compounding. At P/E 20.6x and zero free cash yield, I am paying a full price for a capital-hungry business outside my circle of competence. I will pass.
